title: Colorado Senate Bill 26-189: Automated Decision-Making Technology
author: Colorado General Assembly

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The bill materially develops the cluster’s governance and verification proposition by translating use-context-specific oversight into concrete duties: consequential-use coverage, trained human reviewers with genuine override authority, primary-evidence review, developer documentation, monitoring and record retention. It does not provide empirical evidence that these measures will be effective.

st.t: Automated decisions: Notice and recourse remain distinct rights
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s proposition by establishing separate interaction-stage notice and post-adverse-decision human reconsideration rights, alongside developer duties and public enforcement. It also reinforces the cluster’s warning that version and status must be checked because the supplied summary and legislative text carry conflicting version signals.
qs: The bill establishes consumer notice requirements, mandating that     deployers provide clear and conspicuous notice to consumers at the point     of interaction with a covered ADMT.
The bill     also grants consumers the right to request meaningful human review and     reconsideration following a covered ADMT making a consequential     decision resulting in an adverse outcome.

kp.k: Regulation targets materially influential automated decisions
kp.d: The operative text regulates ADMT that processes personal data and materially influences consequential decisions, rather than AI generally. Material influence requires both a non-de minimis factor used in decision-making and an effect on the outcome. Covered domains include education, employment, Colorado residential real estate, financial or lending services, insurance, health care, and essential government services and public benefits. These are statutory provisions, not empirical findings about professional or market change.

kp.k: Coverage includes employment and materially disadvantageous terms
kp.d: Consumer coverage expressly extends to employees, Colorado-resident job applicants, and individuals whose Colorado opportunities are evaluated by a person doing business in Colorado. Consequential decisions and adverse outcomes encompass certain materially less favorable pricing, compensation, and other terms, not merely outright denial, where the specified effects on access or opportunity are present.

kp.k: Administrative assistance and specified technologies are excluded
kp.d: The text excludes listed infrastructure tools, qualifying non-machine-learning spreadsheets, and tools used solely for specified administrative information-processing purposes. It also excludes summarization or presentation actions that do not generate an inference materially influencing an outcome, along with specified routine, marketing, security, fraud-prevention, and compliance activities. Consumer-facing information or content technologies qualify for an exclusion only under both an intended-use restriction and an acceptable-use policy prohibiting consequential-decision use.

kp.k: Developer status depends on commercialization and intended use
kp.d: Developer coverage includes commercial suppliers, developers of components intended for covered ADMT, and persons intentionally and substantially modifying ADMT into covered systems. Exclusions address qualifying research and internal development, preceding developers following an unaffiliated person's change of intended use, and component integration without actual knowledge. Developer disclosure duties are qualified by the intended, marketed, configured, contracted, sold, or licensed consequential-decision use specified in the text.

kp.k: Developers must document limitations and communicate changes
kp.d: Starting January 1, 2027, developers must supply reasonably understandable documentation covering intended and known inappropriate uses, training-data categories to the extent known, known limitations and risks, appropriate use, monitoring, and meaningful human review where applicable. They must supply information reasonably necessary for deployer disclosures, notify deployers when information is withheld, and communicate material updates and specified changes within a reasonable time. Trade secrets and legally protected information remain protected; public release notes suffice only with direct notice to each deployer.

kp.k: Developers and deployers must retain compliance records
kp.d: Developers must retain reasonably necessary compliance records for at least three years after record creation, including system versions, changelogs, documentation, and update notices. Deployers must retain reasonably necessary compliance records for at least three years after the consequential decision; applicable law may require longer retention. Deployer records may include version identifiers, changelogs, and material mitigation documentation.

kp.k: Notice precedes use; adverse outcomes trigger further disclosure
kp.d: Deployers must provide clear and conspicuous notice before covered use; a prominent public notice reasonably accessible and proximate to the interaction can satisfy this requirement. Within thirty days after an adverse decision, they must explain the decision and ADMT's role, provide a simple process for requesting further system and input information, and explain consumer rights. Some system information is conditional on receipt from the developer. Withholding protected information requires notice, and disclosures must be reasonably accessible to consumers with disabilities and limited English proficiency.

kp.k: Correction and human reconsideration rights have qualifications
kp.d: Following a covered adverse outcome, consumers may request instructions for accessing personal data and correcting factually incorrect or materially inaccurate personal data, plus meaningful human review and reconsideration to the extent commercially reasonable. Correction does not extend to opinions, predictions, scores, or protected evaluations. Meaningful review requires a trained person empowered to approve, modify, or override the decision, considering available primary evidence rather than defaulting to system output, with sufficient information about the output and principal factors but without requiring trade-secret disclosure.

kp.k: Attorney general enforcement includes a conditional cure period
kp.d: Violations constitute deceptive trade practices, with exclusive attorney general enforcement of the specified disclosure, recordkeeping, and consumer-rights requirements. When the attorney general deems cure possible, notice precedes enforcement and a sixty-day cure period applies; demonstrated knowing or repeated violations do not require that period. Annual reporting on enforcement and cure periods begins in January 2028. Subsection 6-1-1706(3), containing these cure and reporting provisions, is repealed January 1, 2030. The text creates no new private right of action and preserves existing remedies.

kp.k: Discrimination liability follows relative developer and deployer fault
kp.d: For existing state-law discrimination actions involving covered decisions, fault is allocated between developers and deployers according to relative fault. Developer liability under this section requires both use within the specified intended or represented uses and material influence on the decision giving rise to the violation. The text preserves deployer responsibility for independent acts and omissions and does not create joint and several liability beyond existing law. Compliance with this part and use of ADMT do not excuse other legal violations.

kp.k: Contracts cannot generally transfer responsibility for own discrimination
kp.d: The text voids developer-deployer contractual provisions indemnifying, defending, or holding a party harmless against covered discrimination damages resulting from that party's own acts or omissions. An exception protects developers where consequential-decision use falls outside the specified intended or represented uses and the developer complied with documentation requirements. Other commercial contract terms remain generally enforceable, and applicable insurance remains available.

kp.k: Implementation centers on January 2027 and sector-sensitive rulemaking
kp.d: The text generally takes effect January 1, 2027 and applies to consequential decisions made on or after that date; specified rulemaking, joinder, appropriation, and related provisions take effect upon passage. The attorney general must adopt rules implementing post-adverse-outcome disclosures and consumer rights by January 1, 2027, with disclosure rules accounting for sector-specific practices. Rulemaking requires stakeholder participation, written comment, and at least one public hearing. The 2026-27 appropriation is $46,190, based on an additional 0.4 FTE.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The Colorado General Assembly's text establishes a regulatory framework for automated technology that materially influences consequential decisions; it does not predict lawyer displacement or changes in legal-service markets.
pts.d: In its own cross-domain setting, the source treats automated predictions, rankings, scores and recommendations as capable of meaningfully influencing individuals' opportunities and material terms. The operative provisions impose developer documentation and update duties, deployer recordkeeping and notice duties, and consumer correction and reconsideration rights. They allocate relative fault between developers and deployers in existing state discrimination actions, restrict contractual indemnification for a party's own covered misconduct, and preserve existing legal obligations. Enforcement of the specified disclosure, recordkeeping and consumer-rights requirements belongs exclusively to the attorney general; the text creates no new private right of action. These are legislative prescriptions rather than empirical findings or market forecasts.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The basis is legislative authority and statutory design, not measured evidence about AI's effects.
pts.d: The supplied text attributes the framework to the Colorado General Assembly and sets out definitions, duties, remedies, exceptions and implementation arrangements. It provides no benchmarks, empirical studies, case examples or quantified estimates of discrimination reduction, consumer benefit, business compliance costs or demand for legal services. Its appropriation of $46,190 for fiscal year 2026–27 assumes an additional 0.4 FTE in the department of law; this is a budget assumption, not evidence of realised effects. Although the supplied title calls it a signed act, the reproduced legislative header describes a revised version including second-reading amendments in the second house; enactment status is not independently established here.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The framework generally takes effect January 1, 2027 and applies to consequential decisions from that date, subject to important scope limits and exceptions.
pts.d: Specified rulemaking, appropriation and other provisions take effect upon passage; disclosure and consumer-rights rules must be adopted by January 1, 2027. Developers retain required records for at least three years after creation, and deployers for at least three years after the consequential decision, unless other law requires longer retention. Adverse-outcome disclosures are generally due within 30 days. A 60-day cure opportunity applies when the attorney general considers cure possible, but knowing or repeated violations need not receive it; the cure/reporting subsection sunsets January 1, 2030, with annual reporting beginning January 2028. Coverage requires material influence rather than incidental or clerical use. Routine administrative and specified other uses are excluded. Human review and reconsideration are qualified by commercial reasonableness, correction does not extend to opinions, predictions, scores or protected evaluations, and disclosures protect trade secrets and legally protected information. Sector-specific exemptions and alternative compliance channels further qualify application.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly affected groups are covered developers and deployers, individuals facing consequential decisions, designated human reviewers and public enforcement authorities.
pts.d: Covered domains encompass education, employment, Colorado residential real estate, financial or lending services, insurance, health care, essential government services and public benefits. Consumer coverage expressly includes employees, Colorado-resident job applicants and individuals whose Colorado opportunities are evaluated by a person doing business in Colorado. Developers must supply relevant information and update notices; deployers must retain records, notify affected individuals and administer applicable requests. A meaningful human reviewer must be trained, consider available primary evidence, have authority to change the decision and not default to the system output. Notices must be reasonably accessible to consumers with disabilities and limited English proficiency. Insurers, HIPAA-covered entities, educational institutions and certain FDA-regulated activities receive differentiated treatment; employment uses remain covered under the stated insurer and health-entity exceptions. The attorney general implements and enforces the framework. No effects on law-firm staffing, fees or productivity are asserted.
